title: The Man
full_review:
"The Man" (New Line) is a distinctly minor action comedy about a nerdy -- but decent -- middle-aged dental products salesman, Andy Fiddler (Eugene Levy), who's mistaken for a stolen arms dealer when he comes to Detroit for a convention.

He's innocently minding his own business at a diner counter when the initial confusion occurs. Before long, Fiddler has become the unwilling partner of federal agent Derrick Vann (Samuel L. Jackson), whose crooked partner has just been murdered in a sting operation against the bad guys, headed by the cold-eyed Joey (Luke Goss). Both the gang and the feds think Andy's a criminal because he once unknowingly purchased a purloined rug in Turkey, and Interpol has him pegged as a wanted man.

Fiddler is an impatiently reluctant party to all this, but as the story develops, he proves more of an asset to Vann, and is able to use his sales skills to good advantage, while a bond develops between the oddest of odd couples.

Director Les Mayfield's film is fitfully amusing, thanks to the chemistry of the two intentionally mismatched stars, but could be much better.

There are positive underlying themes of the importance of friendship, allowing yourself to trust, and putting family first (Andy's a solid family man, who encourages the separated Vann to attend his own daughter's ballet recitals and get back together with his estranged wife).

Nonetheless, the unrelenting stream of expletives, formulaic construction and mostly uninspired dialogue severely undermine what might otherwise have been a recommendable escapade.

At one point, Fiddler lectures Vann on his use of the f-word, suggesting he substitute "for crying out loud" instead. By the end of the film, Vann has taken his advice -- a nice touch, but 80 minutes too late!

On the plus side, the violence is relatively restrained, and some innuendo aside -- Fiddler is arrested at one point, and there's a passing implication of the threat of prison rape -- there is no sexual content.

There's good work from Susie Essman as Vann's boss and Anthony Mackie as a street hustler who reluctantly gives Vann leads.

The film contains excessive crude language, as well as a few instances of rough language and profanity, some action violence, general vulgarity, some sexual innuendo and ethnic humor. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
